title: What a CBDC Is
body:
A central bank digital currency, usually shortened to CBDC, is digital money issued directly by a country's central bank, denominated in that country's currency. It differs from the digital money most people already use: a bank deposit is a claim on a commercial bank, and a card payment moves bank money, while a CBDC is a direct claim on the central bank itself, in digital form. It also differs from cash, which is central bank money in physical form, and from cryptocurrencies, which are generally issued by no central bank and whose value is not set by a government. A CBDC is therefore best understood as cash's digital cousin, not as a new kind of private money.

Method. The working method for this record is a four-way classification. First, ask who issues the money: a central bank, a commercial bank, or nobody in particular. Second, ask what form it takes: physical, account-based digital, or token-based digital. Third, ask who may hold it: the general public, in the retail case, or financial institutions only, in the wholesale case. Fourth, ask what backs its value: the issuing state's currency system, a pool of assets, or market supply and demand. Running any digital money through those four questions places it correctly, and most confusion about CBDCs comes from skipping one of them. The demo classifies four forms of money by issuer and form.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for what a cbdc is. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: cash | issuer: central bank | form: physical; bank deposit | issuer: commercial bank | form: account; retail CBDC | issuer: central bank | form: token; cryptocurrency | issuer: no central issuer | form: token Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record as the starting point for any discussion of digital currency, CBDCs, or programmable money, and before judging any CBDC proposal, since proposals differ sharply once the four questions are answered. Do not use it to claim that any particular CBDC exists or is available where you live, because availability varies widely and changes over time. Do not use it as investment guidance, because a CBDC is a payment instrument, not an investment product. title: Retail and Wholesale CBDCs
body:
CBDC designs split into two broad families: retail and wholesale. A retail CBDC is available to the general public, for everyday payments by households and businesses, much as cash is today. A wholesale CBDC is available only to financial institutions, for settling large payments between banks and other market participants, much as central bank reserves do today. The distinction matters because the two families solve different problems: retail designs raise questions about public access, privacy, and the role of banks, while wholesale designs raise questions about settlement speed, cross-border payments, and market infrastructure.

Method. The working method for this record is a purpose-first comparison. First, name the intended users: everyone, or institutions only. Second, name the payments it must serve: everyday purchases and transfers, or large-value settlement. Third, name the existing system it would sit beside or replace: cash and bank payments in the retail case, reserve accounts and settlement systems in the wholesale case. Fourth, name the hardest design question for each family: public access and privacy for retail, interoperability between institutions and systems for wholesale. The demo sorts a list of design questions into the retail or wholesale family.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for retail and wholesale cbdcs. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: retail -> public access; retail -> privacy tiers; wholesale -> settlement speed; wholesale -> cross-border settlement; retail -> offline use Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record when reading any CBDC announcement, since the announcement's meaning changes entirely with which family it describes. Do not use it to assume a country pursuing one family is pursuing the other, because many central banks explore wholesale designs while remaining undecided on retail. Do not use it as a prediction about which family will prevail, because both remain active areas of work. title: Two-Tier CBDC Distribution
body:
Two-tier distribution is the most widely discussed way of getting a retail CBDC into people's hands. In a two-tier model, the central bank issues the CBDC, and commercial banks, payment firms, and other intermediaries distribute it to the public, handle customer accounts or wallets, and provide customer service. The public therefore deals with familiar firms, while the money itself remains a central bank liability. The alternative, a single-tier model where the public deals directly with the central bank, is discussed far less, because central banks generally do not run retail customer operations.

Method. The working method for this record is a flow tracing exercise. First, the central bank issues CBDC to intermediaries against reserves, so issuance stays with the central bank. Second, intermediaries onboard users, check identity as required, and provide wallets or accounts. Third, users pay each other through intermediaries, with the CBDC moving between wallets. Fourth, intermediaries settle with each other through the central bank, keeping the system balanced. Fifth, customer problems, such as a lost device or a disputed payment, are handled by the intermediary the customer knows, not by the central bank directly. The demo prints the five steps in order.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for two-tier cbdc distribution. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: 1 - central bank issues CBDC; 2 - intermediaries onboard users; 3 - users pay wallet to wallet; 4 - intermediaries settle at the central bank; 5 - intermediaries handle customer service Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record to understand why most CBDC proposals keep banks and payment firms in the picture even though the money is central bank issued. Do not use it to assume every proposal is two-tier, because designs vary and some proposals give intermediaries different roles. Do not use it to claim intermediaries disappear or remain unchanged, because their exact role is one of the main open design questions. title: The Sand Dollar
body:
The Sand Dollar is the Bahamas' digital currency, issued by the Central Bank of The Bahamas, and it is widely described as the first fully launched retail CBDC. Its stated purpose is practical: the Bahamas is an archipelago, and moving physical cash between islands is slow and costly, so a digital form of the Bahamian dollar helps residents pay and transfer money across islands. The Sand Dollar is denominated in Bahamian dollars, distributed through authorized financial institutions, and designed for everyday payments, with tiered wallets that set different holding and transaction limits depending on how much identity information the holder has provided.

Method. The working method for this record is a case reading in four parts. First, the problem is named: cash distribution across many islands is expensive and slow. Second, the issuer and denomination are named: the central bank, in Bahamian dollars. Third, the distribution model is named: authorized intermediaries provide wallets to the public. Fourth, the tiering idea is noted: lighter identity checks go with lower limits, and fuller checks go with higher limits, balancing access against safeguards. The demo prints the four parts of the case as a structured summary.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for the sand dollar. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: issuer : Central Bank of The Bahamas; denomination : Bahamian dollar; distribution : authorized intermediaries; tiering : limits by identity level Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record as a concrete example when discussing what a launched retail CBDC looks like in practice. Do not use it to claim the Sand Dollar's design fits every country, because its island geography shaped its purpose. Do not use it as a source of adoption figures, because this record reports the design, not measured uptake. title: The eNaira
body:
The eNaira is Nigeria's digital currency, issued by the Central Bank of Nigeria, and it is widely described as one of the first launched retail CBDCs in Africa. Its stated purposes include improving payments, supporting financial inclusion for people with limited access to banking, and making government payments and remittances easier to move. The eNaira is denominated in naira, distributed through banks and other intermediaries, and provided through wallets with different tiers, so that people with basic phones and limited identification can still hold a wallet within limits, while fuller identification opens higher limits.

Method. The working method for this record is the same four-part case reading used for the Sand Dollar. First, the problems are named: payment efficiency, inclusion, and the movement of official payments and remittances. Second, the issuer and denomination are named: the central bank, in naira. Third, the distribution model is named: banks and intermediaries provide wallets. Fourth, the tiering idea is noted: lower tiers for basic access, higher tiers for fuller identification. The demo prints the eNaira case in the same four-part shape, so the two launched cases can be compared side by side.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for the enaira. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: issuer : Central Bank of Nigeria; denomination : naira; distribution : banks and intermediaries; tiering : limits by identity level Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record as a second concrete example of a launched retail CBDC, and compare it with the Sand Dollar case to see which design choices repeat and which differ. Do not use it to claim that tiering alone solves inclusion, because access also depends on phones, connectivity, and trust. title: e-CNY Pilots
body:
The e-CNY, also called the digital yuan, is China's retail CBDC, developed by the People's Bank of China and tested through pilots in a growing set of cities and scenarios. Early pilot cities widely reported include Shenzhen, Suzhou, Chengdu, and Xiong'an, and pilot uses have covered everyday retail payments, transport, and government-related payments. The e-CNY is designed as a digital form of the yuan, distributed through a two-tier model in which the central bank issues the currency and commercial banks and other operators provide wallets and services to the public. Its pilots are notable for testing at large scale in live retail settings rather than only in laboratories.

Method. The working method for this record is a pilot reading in four parts. First, the issuer and denomination are named: the People's Bank of China, in yuan. Second, the distribution model is named: two-tier, through banks and operators. Third, the pilot geography and scenarios are listed qualitatively: several cities, everyday retail and transport uses. Fourth, the open questions are noted: how the design balances usability, privacy, and oversight at scale, which pilots are meant to reveal. The demo lists the widely reported early pilot cities and counts them.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for e-cny pilots. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: widely reported early pilot cities: ['Shenzhen', 'Suzhou', 'Chengdu', "Xiong'an"]; count: 4 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record as an example of large-scale live piloting of a retail CBDC. Do not use it to claim the e-CNY is fully launched nationwide on the same terms as the pilots, because pilot terms and availability have changed over time. title: Digital Euro Preparation
body:
The digital euro is the European Central Bank's project to explore a digital form of the euro for the euro area, and it is described by its sponsor as being in investigation and preparation work rather than as a launched currency. The stated motivation is to give people a public digital payment option alongside cash and private payment services, and to preserve the role of central bank money as payments become increasingly digital. Key design questions under study include how the digital euro would be distributed through banks and payment firms, what privacy protections would apply, whether holding limits would be used, and how it would work for payments in shops, online, and between people.

Method. The working method for this record is a preparation reading. First, the project's status is stated honestly: under investigation and preparation, not launched. Second, the motivation is named: a public digital option as cash use changes. Third, the distribution question is named: intermediaries would serve the public, with the central bank issuing. Fourth, the open design questions are listed: privacy, holding limits, offline use, and the treatment of existing payment services. The demo prints the open questions as a checklist for reading future announcements.

title: Fiat-Backed Stablecoins
body:
A fiat-backed stablecoin is a privately issued digital token designed to hold a steady value against a fiat currency, usually by holding reserves, such as bank deposits or short-term government securities, equal to the tokens in circulation. Holders can typically redeem tokens for the underlying currency through the issuer, and the token moves on a blockchain or similar ledger, which makes it usable in digital asset markets and for transfers. The design's credibility rests entirely on the reserves and on whether holders can actually redeem: a token whose reserves are unclear, insufficient, or hard to verify is a claim, not a stable store of value.

Method. The working method for this record is a reserve check. First, the peg is named: which currency, and at what rate, the token aims to track. Second, the reserve claim is named: what assets the issuer says back the tokens. Third, the redemption path is named: who can redeem, how quickly, and on what terms. Fourth, the verification is named: what independent attestation or audit the issuer provides, and how recent it is. The demo computes a reserve ratio from clearly labeled illustrative example inputs, showing how a shortfall would appear as a ratio below one.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for fiat-backed stablecoins. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: reserve ratio: 0.95; fully backed: False Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record to evaluate any fiat-backed stablecoin by its reserves and redemption path, not by its marketing. Do not use it to claim any particular stablecoin is safe, because reserve quality and redemption terms differ sharply between issuers and change over time. Do not use it as investment guidance. title: Programmable Money and Conditional Payments
body:
Programmable money is money whose movement can be governed by rules executed automatically, so that a payment happens only when stated conditions are met. The clearest example is a conditional payment: funds are set aside, and released only when an agreed event is confirmed, such as delivery of goods, completion of a service, or arrival of a date. Programmability can be built at different layers: the money itself can carry rules, or ordinary money can be wrapped in a program, such as an escrow or smart contract, that enforces the conditions. The distinction matters, because rules built into the money itself affect everyone who holds it, while rules built around a payment affect only that payment.

Method. The working method for this record is a condition evaluator. First, the payment's conditions are written as checkable statements, such as goods delivered and inspection passed. Second, the funds are set aside, so the payment cannot be spent twice or withdrawn early. Third, evidence for each condition is checked, by a person, a sensor reading, or another system, depending on the design. Fourth, the payment releases only when every condition is satisfied, and returns or holds the funds otherwise. The demo evaluates a small conditional payment whose delivery condition is met and whose inspection condition is not, and shows the payment correctly held.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for programmable money and conditional payments. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: conditions: {'goods delivered': True, 'inspection passed': False}; payment released: False Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record to understand what programmability adds beyond ordinary scheduled payments, and to ask, for any programmable proposal, who writes the rules and who can change them. Do not use it to claim programmable money restricts how ordinary cash can be spent, because conditional rules in the designs discussed here attach to specific payments, not to all holdings. Do not use it as legal advice about escrow or contract terms. title: Offline CBDC Payments
body:
Offline CBDC payments are payments made without a network connection at the moment of payment, using stored value on a device such as a card or phone, with the transaction settled or synchronized later when connectivity returns. Offline capability matters because cash works without connectivity, and a digital replacement that fails in a tunnel, a rural area, or a power cut is a worse payment instrument for the people who need it most. The hard problem is preventing double spending: without a live check, a payer could try to spend the same stored value twice before the system synchronizes, so offline designs need limits, secure hardware, or deferred settlement rules that bound the risk.

Method. The working method for this record is a stored-value simulation. First, a purse is loaded with a balance and a per-payment limit. Second, payments deduct from the purse locally, without any network check, and each payment is recorded. Third, the purse refuses payments that exceed the balance or the per-payment limit. Fourth, when connectivity returns, the recorded payments synchronize, and any discrepancy is flagged for the issuer. The demo runs three local payments against a small purse and shows the remaining balance.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for offline cbdc payments. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: pay 10 -> accepted | balance now 40; pay 15 -> accepted | balance now 25; pay 30 -> REFUSED | balance now 25 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record to evaluate offline claims in any CBDC proposal, by asking how double spending is bounded and what happens when synchronization reveals a problem. Do not use it to claim any particular CBDC offers general offline payments today, because offline designs remain under testing in most projects. Do not use it as a security assessment of any specific device. title: Privacy Tiers in CBDC Design
body:
Privacy tiers are the idea that a CBDC can offer different levels of privacy for different sizes and types of payment, rather than a single all-or-nothing rule. Small everyday payments might be designed for minimal data collection, similar in spirit to cash, while larger payments carry fuller identity and reporting requirements, similar to bank transfers. The tiering is meant to balance two real concerns: ordinary people should not have every small purchase tracked, and payment systems must still deter crime and satisfy anti-money-laundering rules. Where the lines are drawn, and who sets them, is one of the most contested design questions in CBDC work.

Method. The working method for this record is a tier table. First, payment sizes are grouped into tiers, such as small, medium, and large, using illustrative thresholds that a design might choose. Second, each tier is assigned a data rule: what identity information is collected, what transaction data is retained, and who can see it. Third, the tier boundaries are stated openly, so users know which tier their payment falls into before they pay. Fourth, the table is checked for a basic fairness property: smaller payments do not carry heavier data requirements than larger ones. The demo prints a three-tier table and checks that ordering property.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for privacy tiers in cbdc design. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: small -> minimal data; medium -> basic identity; large -> full identity and reporting; data grows with size: True Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record to read CBDC privacy claims critically, by asking which tier a given payment falls into rather than accepting a blanket privacy claim. Do not use it to claim any particular CBDC guarantees cash-like anonymity, because most designs explicitly retain some data for oversight. Do not use it as legal advice about privacy rights in any jurisdiction. title: Cross-Border CBDC Bridges
body:
Cross-border CBDC bridges are experimental arrangements that let CBDCs from different countries settle payments between each other without passing through the slow correspondent banking chain that international payments use today. One widely discussed example is mBridge, a project of the Bank for International Settlements Innovation Hub together with several central banks, which tests a shared platform where participating CBDCs can be exchanged directly. The promise is faster and cheaper cross-border settlement; the difficulties are governance, agreeing on common rules, handling different legal systems, and deciding who operates the shared platform.

Method. The working method for this record is a bridge walk-through. First, the payer's bank holds the payer's CBDC and the payee's bank will receive the payee's CBDC. Second, the two CBDCs are exchanged on the shared platform at an agreed rate, in a single coordinated step, so neither side pays before the other side's payment is secured. Third, the platform records the exchange and each central bank updates its own ledger. Fourth, compliance checks, such as sanctions and identity screening, run before settlement, not after. The demo prints the four steps in order for a payment between two illustrative participants.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for cross-border cbdc bridges. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. Use and limits. Use this record to understand why cross-border CBDC work is described as promising but experimental. Do not use it to claim any bridge is a live production system for general payments, because the projects discussed here are experimental platforms. title: CBDCs Versus Cryptocurrencies
body:
CBDCs and cryptocurrencies are often confused because both are digital, but they differ on the questions that matter most: who issues them, what gives them value, and who is accountable when something goes wrong. A CBDC is issued by a central bank, denominated in the national currency, and its value tracks that currency by design. A cryptocurrency is typically issued by no central bank, its value is set by market supply and demand, and accountability is spread across its developers, miners or validators, exchanges, and users, with no single institution guaranteeing redemption. Stablecoins sit between the two in some respects, being privately issued but designed to track a fiat currency through reserves, as the stablecoin record explains.

Method. The working method for this record is a comparison matrix. First, issuer is compared: central bank versus no central issuer versus private issuer. Second, value anchor is compared: national currency versus market price versus reserve pool. Third, redemption is compared: a CBDC is the currency itself, a stablecoin promises redemption through its issuer, and most cryptocurrencies offer no redemption at all. Fourth, oversight is compared: CBDCs sit inside the central bank's mandate, stablecoins face varying regulation, and cryptocurrencies face a patchwork that differs by jurisdiction. The demo prints the matrix row by row.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for cbdcs versus cryptocurrencies. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: CBDC | issuer: central bank | value anchor: national currency; stablecoin | issuer: private issuer | value anchor: reserve pool; cryptocurrency | issuer: no central issuer | value anchor: market price Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record to correct the common error of treating CBDCs as just another cryptocurrency. Do not use it to claim any cryptocurrency is or is not a good investment, because this record is about institutional design, not investment merit. Do not use it as legal advice about the regulatory status of any token in any jurisdiction. title: CBDCs and Financial Inclusion
body:
Financial inclusion is one of the most cited motivations for retail CBDCs: people without bank accounts, people in remote areas, and people who receive remittances from abroad may gain a digital payment option that does not require a traditional bank relationship. Tiered wallets, basic phones, agent networks, and offline capability are the design features most often linked to inclusion, because each lowers a specific barrier: tiering lowers the identification barrier, basic-phone support lowers the device barrier, agents lower the distance barrier, and offline use lowers the connectivity barrier. Inclusion, however, depends on more than the currency design: trust, literacy, fees, and connectivity all shape whether people actually use a new payment option.

Method. The working method for this record is a barrier map. First, the barriers are listed: identification, device, distance, connectivity, cost, and trust. Second, each barrier is matched to the design feature meant to lower it, or marked unmatched where no feature addresses it. Third, the map is checked for unmatched barriers, because an inclusion claim that ignores an unmatched barrier is incomplete. The demo maps six barriers to features and reports which barriers remain unmatched in the illustrative map.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for cbdcs and financial inclusion. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: identification -> tiered wallets; device -> basic-phone support; distance -> agent networks; connectivity -> offline use; cost -> UNMATCHED; trust -> UNMATCHED; unmatched barriers: ['cost', 'trust'] Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record to evaluate inclusion claims for any CBDC proposal, by asking which barriers its design actually lowers. Do not use it to claim a CBDC by itself creates inclusion, because the surrounding services and conditions matter as much as the currency. Do not use it as a source of inclusion statistics for any country. title: Disintermediation Debate
body:
The disintermediation debate asks what happens to commercial banks if households and firms can hold money directly as CBDC instead of as bank deposits. Banks lend from deposits, so a large shift from deposits to CBDC could, in principle, reduce bank funding and lending, especially in a crisis when people might move money quickly to the perceived safety of central bank money. Central banks studying CBDCs discuss several mitigations: holding limits on CBDC wallets, tiered remuneration that discourages large holdings, and design choices that keep CBDC primarily a payment instrument rather than a savings vehicle. The debate is unresolved, which is why limits and tiers appear in so many CBDC proposals.

Method. The working method for this record is an illustrative shift calculation. First, a bank's deposit base and a hypothetical share shifting to CBDC are stated as clearly labeled illustrative example inputs, not as figures about any real bank. Second, the shifted amount and the remaining deposit base are computed. Third, the result is read qualitatively: a small share is a funding ripple, a large share is a funding shock, and the boundary between them depends on the bank's other funding sources. The demo computes the remaining base for a five percent illustrative shift and a twenty percent illustrative shift, side by side.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for disintermediation debate. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: shift 5% -> deposits remaining: 950; shift 20% -> deposits remaining: 800 Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record to understand why holding limits are discussed in CBDC design, and to ask, of any proposal, how it handles a rapid shift in stress. Do not use the illustrative numbers as predictions about any real bank or CBDC, because they are arithmetic examples only. Do not use it as investment or banking advice. title: Tokenized Deposits Versus CBDCs
body:
Tokenized deposits are commercial bank deposits represented as digital tokens on a shared ledger, so that they can move with the programmability and settlement properties of tokenized money while remaining claims on commercial banks rather than on the central bank. They are sometimes discussed as an alternative or complement to CBDCs: where a CBDC gives the public direct central bank money in digital form, tokenized deposits keep the existing two-tier banking structure and tokenize the bank-money layer instead. Some proposals combine the two, using wholesale CBDC for settlement between banks while customers hold tokenized deposits. The field is early, and the designs, legal treatment, and interoperability questions are still being worked out.

Method. The working method for this record is a layer comparison. First, the claim is named: central bank for a CBDC, commercial bank for a tokenized deposit. Second, the holder's counterparty risk is named: the central bank in one case, a commercial bank in the other. Third, the settlement asset is named: CBDC itself in a CBDC system, or tokenized deposits settling in wholesale CBDC or reserves in a combined design. Fourth, the maturity question is named: CBDC pilots are further along in several countries, while tokenized deposit proposals are mostly at design and pilot discussion stage. The demo prints the comparison row by row.

Worked example. The demo program attached to this record carries out a concrete calculation for tokenized deposits versus cbdcs. Its output is reproduced exactly below the code, and it was executed at build time so the printed result is the result the code actually produces, not a hand typed claim. The output reads: CBDC | claim on: central bank | settles in: CBDC itself; tokenized deposit | claim on: commercial bank | settles in: wholesale CBDC or reserves Readers who run the same code with the same inputs will obtain the same output, which is the reproducibility standard every record here must meet.

Use and limits. Use this record to distinguish tokenized deposits from CBDCs when proposals blur the two. Do not use it to claim tokenized deposits are available as a general retail product, because the designs discussed here are proposals and pilots. Do not use it as investment guidance.
